sections.html:
San Miguel County is a long, narrow county in northeastern New Mexico that runs from the Great Plains to the Rocky Mountains. The only city, and the county seat, is Las Vegas. The 2020 census found 27,201 residents spread over 4,736 square miles. Pecos and part of Mosquero are villages, and smaller communities include Sapello, Rociada, Montezuma, Ilfeld, San Miguel del Vado and Tererro.

Places are small and far apart. A house in Sapello or Rociada is a long way from services in Las Vegas, so sellers out there should be ready for buyers' questions about road access, utilities and boundary lines before any price is agreed.

The Assessor and the Treasurer share a building and work in sequence. The Assessor values property and builds the tax roll, then hands it to the Treasurer in the fall.

San Miguel County Assessor500 W. National Ave., Suite 105, Las Vegas, NM 87701505-454-1430

Walk-in hours at both county offices are 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., Monday through Friday. The Treasurer also accepts online payment through a bill-pay site and by phone at 877-690-3729 using Jurisdiction #4115. If online payment gives you trouble, call 505-425-9377 so the payment is not doubled.

Pay the first half by November 10 or it turns delinquent on December 11. Pay the second half by April 10 or it turns delinquent on May 11. After that, late fees land on the 11th of every month against what is still owed, even when you have made partial payments.

Property is auctioned by the state in the third year of delinquency, and the Treasurer can take payments on an account only until it is placed on the state's list.

The Assessor's yearly calendar runs on its own track: an assessment period from January 1 to February 28, tax rates entered on September 1, the tax roll going to the Treasurer on October 1, and a mass year rollover starting December 1. Notices of Valuation are dated June 1, but the date printed on your own notice is the one that sets your deadline.

A San Miguel County auction is on the state's calendar for November 19, 2026, starting at 10:00 a.m. People who want to bid register from 8 a.m. until the sale begins. The Taxation and Revenue Department's auction page links to the advertisement and to registration.

Everything sells as is and refunds are not given. Bidding opens at the taxes, penalty, interest and costs owed. The winner receives a tax deed, which is the same as a quitclaim deed, and only the tax lien is cleared. Any other lien on the property stays.

The County Treasurer or Assessor can give you the sale list. Redemption does not exist in New Mexico, though Section 7-38-70 allows a two-year court challenge to a sale. That remedy is narrow. Paying the balance, or selling the house, before the sale is much safer.

Protests go to the Assessor in writing. Section 7-38-24 NMSA 1978 sets the deadline at April 1 or thirty days after the notice of valuation is mailed, whichever is later. State your name and address, describe the property, and say why the value is off and what it should be. The state's protest pamphlet reprints the statute.

The Assessor's page offers a protest petition and pamphlet in English and Spanish. Staff are reappraising across the county, and appraisers carry county identification and wear safety vests, so a visit from one is not unusual.

Three board members at the county valuation protests board decide each protest within 180 days, and district court takes appeals filed within thirty days. Separately, residential value may rise only to the greater of 103 percent of last year or 106.1 percent of two years back, except after a sale or new improvements.

Identify each unpaid year, confirm the parcel is not already on the state's list, and get a payoff figure to the title company. The county does not prorate property tax, so the closing paperwork splits the year between you and the buyer. For a mid-year sale, check with the Treasurer on how it is handled.

  • Call the Treasurer at 505-425-9376 for the balance on each year.
  • Find out whether the parcel is on the state's current delinquent list.
  • Check the Assessor's records for the owner of record, especially on inherited land passed through a family without a recorded deed.
  • Selling a mobile home along with the land? Ask the Assessor if a tax release is required.

Cash Home Buyers purchases San Miguel County houses in as-is condition, even those with back taxes, murky title papers or repairs the owner cannot afford. You get a written cash offer, and the decision stays with you.

sections.h2: Before listing a San Miguel County property
sections.html:
Distance and old paperwork are the usual causes of delay in this county, more than tax rules. A few steps taken early help.

  1. Walk the property lines or locate the survey. Buyers for land in Sapello, Rociada or Tererro often ask where the boundaries sit.
  2. Confirm how access works, including the road and any shared lane, and which utilities serve the house.
  3. Ask the Assessor who is the owner of record. If land passed through a family without a recorded deed, fix that before any contract is signed.
  4. Collect the Treasurer's balance for all years, and note the 11th-of-the-month fee schedule if anything is past due.
  5. Give the title company all of it at once, so one call produces the payoff and a clear list of what is left to do.

Selling for cash as-is takes away most of the repair and showing work, though the title and tax steps are identical to those in a regular sale.

When you meet a buyer or the title company, bring a copy of your deed, the most recent tax bill and any Notice of Valuation you received. If you filed a protest, bring that petition and any reply from the Assessor. For inherited property, bring whatever shows how title passed to you, whether a deed, a court order or an affidavit, because the Assessor's records may still show an earlier owner.

If you are not sure which year a payment was applied to, call the Treasurer at 505-425-9376 and ask for a statement by year. Keep that statement with your closing file.

faqs.q: Where are the San Miguel County tax offices?
faqs.a: Both the Treasurer and the Assessor are at 500 W. National Ave. in Las Vegas, NM 87701. The Treasurer is in Suite 111 and the Assessor in Suite 105.

faqs.q: When are San Miguel County property taxes due?
faqs.a: November 10 is the first-half due date, with delinquency on December 11. April 10 is the second-half date, with delinquency on May 11. Late fees keep adding on the 11th of each month to past due balances.

faqs.q: When does San Miguel County property go to tax auction?
faqs.a: In the third year of delinquency the state can auction a property. The next San Miguel County auction is dated November 19, 2026, at 10:00 a.m.

faqs.q: How do I protest my San Miguel County property value?
faqs.a: Send the County Assessor a written petition by April 1 or thirty days after the notice of valuation is mailed, whichever is later. Explain the error and give your own figure.

faqs.q: Can I sell a San Miguel County house that has back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The closing pays the unpaid balance from your proceeds. Selling ahead of a state auction lets you control how it ends.
